content.title: The Repository and the Working Tree
content.hook: When you use Git, there are two important ideas:
content.context:
**Working tree:** the files you are currently looking at and editing.

**Repository:** the Git-managed history that records project states and changes.

The working tree answers:

> “What does my project look like right now?”

The repository answers:

> “What history has been recorded?”
goals: Distinguish the project files you are currently changing from the Git history that records versions of the project.

content.question:
You change a file in the working tree but have not recorded that change yet.

Which statement is true?

options.text: The file on disk changed, but the new change is not yet part of the recorded Git history.
Every Git user on the project immediately receives the change.
The change automatically becomes permanent history.
The change is impossible to lose because Git has already committed it.

feedback.correct: Editing a file and recording that edit are different operations.
feedback.incorrect: Editing a file and recording that edit are different operations.

content.title: `git status`
content.text:
One of the most useful commands is:

```bash
git status
```

Think of it as asking Git:

> “What is different about my working tree right now?”

A simplified result might look like:

```text
modified:   src/app.js
modified:   styles.css
```

That does not mean those files have been committed. It means Git sees changes that are not yet part of the latest recorded project state.

content.question:
Suppose you edit only `src/app.js`.

Then `git status` reports:

```text
modified:   src/app.js
```

What should you conclude?

options.text: The working tree differs from the recorded state for that file.
A pull request has been opened.

feedback.correct: Status tells you about the relationship between your working files and the recorded state.
feedback.incorrect: Status tells you about the relationship between your working files and the recorded state.

content.title: The first engineering habit
content.text:
Before committing, run:

```bash
git status
```

Do not treat Git as a vending machine where you blindly type commands until it stops complaining.

Use each command as a question.

```text
git status  → What changed?
git diff    → What exactly changed?
git log     → What history exists?
```

You are not memorizing commands. You are building an investigation vocabulary.

content.question:
A file shows as modified.

What does that **not** tell you yet?

options.text: That the file is different from the recorded state.
That you should inspect the change before recording it.
That Git is aware of a difference.

feedback.correct: `git status` tells you that something changed. You need another inspection step to understand the actual change.
feedback.incorrect: `git status` tells you that something changed. You need another inspection step to understand the actual change.
